A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should it be easier to get divorce in the UK?

Opinions:
1. Yes it should be easier to get a divorce in the UK, so that the process does not take as long as the current system. The emotional stress on the couple is too much with the current system. A quicker process would help with the mental health of the couple involved.
2. I think that the only winners when a couple seeks a divorce are the solicitors. When I say it should be easier, I mean that once people have reached a decision to divorce equally, not lust on a whim.
If the couple both agree, and it is amicable, then there should be no need for solicitors with their exorbitant fees.
There should be a series of forms, completed by both parties, and job done.
3. I do not have a strong opinion on this matter as I do not know the current difficulties with obtaining a divorce in the UK. Therefore, I will present the general view that it should be easy to get divorced and not involve mountains of money and extended legal battles. Divorce as a money-making opportunity for an aggrieved party seems like an outdated idea and there should be less limitations for two partners deciding to end their legal partnership. 
4. Yes it should be. The current process is drawn out for far too long, and for what reason other than administerial processes or perhaps so lawyers can get more cash for their paper pushing, this is hardly fair on either party who are going through an emotional moment in their lives.
People do not need financial stressors added to the mix. 
5. In some ways I think divorce should be easier to get in the UK, however I think there would be bad points to allowing divorce to be easier. If divorce was easier to obtain in the UK people whom were in bad relationships would be able to be free from that trauma much quicker and sooner, and make a fresh start. I also think divorce should be made cheaper, as the costs can be off putting to people who can't afford. However, I think that if divorce was easier to obtain then people would seek divorce instead of trying to work on their relationship first.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should the government provide universal free childcare from birth?

Opinions:
1. Universal free childcare will aid working parents with the cost of childcare, so that they can return to work, or increase the working hours. This will help ease the financial burden of the costs involved. 
2. The role of the state should be to care for its citizens, & that role extends to child birth/care.  It is a proven fact that caring for children helps with their development & health, providing it for free means it helps to give a minimum care to all children & helps free one of the parents (who may have given up work) to get back into the workplace.
3. I think the government should provide universal free childcare from birth. Many parents struggle with the financial burden of childcare as the prices are so high, especially now in the cost of living crisis. When parents take maternity or paternity leave, they receive less, if any at all, pay. This can cause parents to have to go back to work before they want to, just to afford to live, including childcare costs. Parents would be happier and able to spend more time with their young children. In addition, expensive childcare can stop people from working full time jobs as they need to be able to look after their children themselves which has a negative impact on businesses. There would be more opportunity for jobs if childcare was free as more childcare facilities would open.
4. Yes, it could be means tested as the wealthier would probably afford to pay for it. Parents should get support back to work if that is their choice, but I also feel this could put pressure on parents to return to work before they are ready and this could impact on the child and parent mental health
5. I don't necessarily think it should be free but when most people are paying more for their childcare costs, to allow them to work, than they are their mortgage, I think it should be subsidised. I don't want to see cheap childcare neither. It needs to be high quality for the future generation to thrive and childcare workers should be paid more than minimum wage. I feel that investing in future generations will pay off by increasing economic productivity. Many people will work for free in effect as they may have a job which they need to hold onto. I myself, am fortunate in that working is economically more viable than staying home with my children but this means that someone else looks after my child. Whilst I see pros and cons with this, it isn't right that some people - mainly women - are forced into giving up their careers as the childcare costs outweigh their income. I pay a third of my salary on childcare and it does stop people having more children

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should we give aid to other countries?

Opinions:
1. The United Kingdom population has a reasonable level of health and quality of life and the population could be considered comfortable. This is due to some factors (climate, natural resources and historical economic advantage, for example). Other countries have lower levels of these qualities through no "fault" of their own so this difference should be made up through foreign aid from the btter off countries of which the United Kingdom is one..
2. Yes, we should give aid to other countries - we are in a privileged position of being one of the richer countries in the world, and we need to do our bit to help others less-privileged. It is just luck that anyone is born in a country where they can access clean water, shelter, food, and adequate healthcare, but everyone is a human being and should have equal rights and equal opportunities. If every rich country supported the poorer countries, they could become better and healthier, and life could be fairer for everyone. 
3. I think in principle we should give aid to other countries. The foreign aid we give is often a minute amount of the government's budget and stopping that wouldn't really free up enough money to help us out. In fact a lot of the foreign aid we give is in order to develop infrastructure such as ports/bridges and roads which benefit the global economy and us in turn. I don't think foreign aid is a purely philanthropical pursuit but more of an economic investment. My only issue is giving this aid to nations who cannot guarantee that it will land in the right hands.
4. I feel that we should give aid to other countries that need aid. But we should also be providing for the needy in our conutry too. I hear about giving aid to countries where the governments are corrupt, or that don't seem to need aid, and we should be enabling countries to help themselves in the longer term too
5. I think we should not give aid to other countries. We have a budget deficit every year and should be aiming to not have a deficit. Our country has record levels of debt so is borrowing money to pay for this aid.  I think the money should be spent on veterans, homeless people, animals.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should Britain remove the statue of Winston Churchill from Parliament Square?

Opinions:
1. I do not believe Britain should remove the statue of Winston Churchill. Churchill is a symbol and a key figure of Britain's past and massively influential in our victory in WW2. Although, I do agree with some issues surrounding Churchill, mainly the effects the war had on Bengal. The statue is apart of our British history and we should look back at our faults and learn from them, not pretend that they didn't exist. 
2. I think it's important that the statue remains as Winston Churchill was a key part of British history in the middle of the 20th century.  His tenure took place in a hugely significant period of British history and WWII and I think it's important that this is recognised.  Further, to remove a statue is to try and erase what happened, and to devalue aspects of his importance to life during the war.
3. Winston Churchill was instrumental in ensuring that the Nazi's were defeated in world war 2 and he should therefore be given credit for that. However, he also made some bad errors when it came to the famine in Bhopal  which led to millions of people dying. Also, I believe he allowed Kenyan people to be tortured. I therefore believe that he did some good and bad things and consequently do not have a strong opinion on whether he should be glorified or not. A statue is in any case not something I personally care much about.
4. I think the Statue is the symbol for Britain's  victory in world war II. He also served as a Prime Minister twice in Britain. So remembering the great soldier is must for any country.
5. No, we shouldn't remove it. Churchill was a very important part of British history, being prime minister during the second world war and he played a very important part in preventing the Nazi invasion of Britain. Although he is now considered  to have held some racist views, these were probably considered socially 'normal' at that time.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should we ban the sale of petrol and diesel cars by 2030?

Opinions:
1. Providing we can commit to supplying a reliable electricity grid then I am not averse to this.  However, if the creation of the electricity results in being every bit as polluting as the use of petrol and diesel then it seems that nothing will change with regard to climate.
2. I personally believe we should however we need to make sure that there are enough reliable and cheap alternatives so this doesn't impact those who do not have the money to get rid of their cars and to buy a new one. However we should be banning this as they have far too much of a negative environmental impact, and we need to take action quickly before it's too late. A lot of the time, these cars are unnecessary.
3. I think we should ban the production of petrol and diesel for sure by 2030, and roll out more affordable, electric options, with an increase of charging points, and a by product of this will be a reduce in sales of petrol and diesel cars. I wouldn't an
4. Probably not by 2030 but there should be a concerted effort towards a ban as soon as possible beyond that date. At the moment battery production and infrastructure for alternative vehicles isn't up to speed so it is unrealistic to set a definite date at this point. Plus, there also needs to be a much improved syste of public transport to provide a viable alternative to the private vehicle. Again, this isn't feasible, especially in rural areas.
5. This country does not have the infrastructure in place to enforce the use of electric cars.  I don't feel that we will be ready by 2030.  Electric cars are also too expensive for a lot of people to buy currently and with the economic issues we have we would be making it impossible for a lot of people to own a car.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Is it ethical for a person to live in a way that harms the environment?

Opinions:
1. I think that it's unethical to deliberately harm the environment. However, it is not always easy to see how regular and irregular activities cause harm. It's also difficult to calculate whether changes in behavior are always beneficial or causing some other harm we are not aware of. 
2. I think it is not ethical for to live in a way that harms the environment. By ensuring people ethical it ensures that it will not harm the environment. Therefore it ensures it is vital to follow this.. 
3. It really depends on how much a persons way of life is harming the environment. If there way of life is no worse than anyone else then it is ethical for them to live that way. We shouldn't be controlling how people live their lives. If we want people to help the environment then we should be encouraging them. Telling people it's not ethical to live in a certain way won't help at all. 
4. The way in which a person lives, providing it's law abiding and not harmful to others is up to them. There is a lot of ambiguity as to the actual impact of things like personal recycling when stacked up against corporate malpractice in this area, so it's understandable if a person doesn't want to be part of what they may see as a futile exercise. While I personally do think individuals have a collective responsibility I also don't blame people who don't care.
5. No, people should respect the environment they live in. It is because of this environment that the human gets to live. In the long run, if no respect is given to the environment, people, flora and fauna will all suffer. Global warming is already becoming an issue so everyone needs to take action to prevent harm to the environment now.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should parents be required to pay for their kids' college education?

Opinions:
1. I strongly feel that parents should not be required to pay for their kids' college education. This would have a disastrous consequences for social mobility in a society which is already run by an elite group of people. It would increase the barriers for talented, bright young people to access higher education. Society needs a broad range of educated young people to allow it to flourish and grow. Why should education only be available to those who can afford it or prepared to go into debt to pay the fees? 
2. a tough question as is if fair for the state to pay for all those to continue their education. One thing is for sure that having to pay for your childs education puts those children from a lower income at a disadvantage. Indeed those from a higher income family at a better advantage and on the disparity continues through out the generations. Eat the rich.
So it probably makes sense to have some payments for lower income families in bandings rather than all or nothing in my view.
3. No. This would create a completely unfair disadvantage to low income families. Not to mention the impact this would have on children who have spent time in the care system or are coming from abusive families. Children and young people should be given fair and equitable access to higher education, not dependent on their parent's income. This would mean incredibly talented and intelligent children missing out on the opportunity to fulfil their potential, and creating further stress for already struggling families.
4. definitely parents should be required to pay for their  kids college education
5. I do believe that everyone should contribute towards their own education costs, but I feel there should be support and funding for everyone who needs additional help. We do need to support poorer families with the cost of college education which might otherwise be unaffordable to avoid people being disadvantaged.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should we encourage high-earning students to stay in the UK by offering them special scholarships?

Opinions:
1. I think it is less about the fact they are high earning and more to do with the profession they are undertaking. We need to do more in tis country to encourage medical professionals to stay for example and I do believe this should be a primary area of focus. Generally speaking also, the more a person earns, the more they pay in taxes so will be good for the economic state of the country also.
2. Encouraging high-earning students to stay in the UK would be beneficial - however, offering them financial scholarships would be a severe waste of money. Instead, universities and the job market should be appealing to students, and they should naturally want to stay in the UK and continue to contribute to the country.
3. I believe high earning students should be offered scholarships to stay in the UK. They most likely have special skill sets to enable them to be high earners and therefor could be valuable to the UK economy. They could then go on to train others with their skills and spread their knowledge to others in the UK. 
4. Offering high earning students scholarships to stay in the UK could be beneficial to the countries economy and overall development. They could go on to create innovative businesses and job opportunities contributing to the UK's growth and success. 
5. I think high-earning students will make their own mind up on which country they wish to work in. I see no harm in offering them special scholarships but I don't believe that alone, will  encourage them to stay in this country. Political, environmental and standard of living could also play a part in their choice.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Is there a good reason for the state to fund the arts?

Opinions:
1. I think arts is important as it helps to promote local culture and people to express creativity. However I think in the current climate its not of high importance given the turmoil that is happening the world with rising energy prices, inflation, cost of living and fuel.
2. Yes, I believe there is a good reason. Arts are very important for creativity, crtitical thinking, and quality leisure. For example, reading supports good communication skills. 
3. Yes, the arts are an integral part of a society's culture. The arts are a way to give a voice to those who may not have one and state funding this would particularly help this cause with many from disadvanteged backgrounds being able to participate. The arts are also an integral part of freedom of expression, having been historically attacked and repressed during times of fascism, the arts are important if we want to keep society both fair and free. The arts are also important outlets for improving mental wellbeing and could help alleviate some of the depression we see in our society.
4. yes the arts are criminally underfunded as things stand and they are in despereate need of funding, the arts play a vital role in our lives and by being funded by the goverment it would give more people access to this
5. there isnt much good reason for the state to fund arts. it is a waste of money. art is subjective so not everyone likes it. state money could be spent on more important things

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should the BBC be funded by TV license fees, or should it be privately funded?

Opinions:
1. I don't have a strong opinion on this topic but I believe the BBC should be privately funded
2. A privately funded BBC would result in vastly increased commercialisation, and a ratings chase, which isn't entirely what the BBC is about. While the BBC's funding does need to be examined to ensure it is fit for purpose in the modern age, the BBC's remit to inform, educate, and entertain, has made it one of the highest regarded and popular broadcasters in the world. Playing to the BBC's strengths by insuring it has the funding to fulfil this purpose is clearly the way to go; an undersized commercial broadcaster competing with the likes of Netflix would bring little benefit. The BBC also has a large amount of news and factual output, which would not be a great money maker, and it would be a net negative to lose such an important and neutral news broadcaster.
3. BBC should be funded privately like the other channels such as ITV, Channel 4 and so on i don't understand why we have to pay for TV license.
4. Sort of neutral on this. Those in favour of the TV license fee argue that it provides a stable source of funding that allows the BBC to remain independent and produce high-quality programming without the influence of advertisers or corporate interests. Those who oppose the license fee argue that it is an outdated model and that the BBC should also be able to compete in the marketplace like other media organisations. I don't have a strong opinion here since it depends on all sorts of factors such as public's willingness to pay for the service and the government's priorities for the media sector
5. The BBC should be privately funded. We don't pay for other freeview channels. We still have to watch BBC advertise their own programmes in between breaks.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should businesses be obliged to provide private space for breastfeeding mothers?

Opinions:
1. Breastfeeding should be allowed anywhere, and should be encouraged. Business should have a moral obligation to assist women with privacy where possible. However, there may be circumstances where this is not practical, such as very small premises, or where space or private rooms are not available. Therefore I would recommend business be encouraged to offer breastfeeding spaces where appropriate, but that this is not mandated in law.
2. I think it depends on what type of business' it is, a Cafe and Restaurants  where you go to eat and drink should have a area to breastfeed a child. Where a bank for example I wouldnt think its needed.
3. I don't believe businesses should be obliged to provide private space for breastfeeding mothers. A place of business should primarily be a place of business, and not concern itself with breastfeeding mothers. There are numerous other places for breastfeeding mothers to go and care for their child. Equally, an infant shouldn't be in a place of business, so I'm not sure why the space should even be needed.
4. I don't think mothers tend to take their babies to work with them, so this isn't a major topic in my eyes. If they need to pump breastmilk this could be done before work. If the workplace has the space to provide a room, then this would be good, but I don't think it's essential.
5. providing private spaces for breastfeading mothers can also benefit businesses. It helps build a positive reputation, attract and retain customers who prioritise family friendly establishments, and enchance overall customer satisfaction. Additionally, creating a comfortable space for breastfeading can encaurage mothers to spend more time in a business establishment.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Should the UK change its asylum seeking policy to make it easier to enter the country?

Opinions:
1. If the UK truly sees itself as an influential global power, it must step up and change its asylum seeking policy. There are numerous ongoing humanitarian crises throughout the world, and the only one where the UK seems to show compassion is with those fleeing war-torn Ukraine. Why not the same level of compassion for asylum seekers from elsewhere in the world. As part of the G7, the UK must take it's fair share of asylum seekers. As an island, it will always be difficult to make it to the UK to claim asylum in comparison with continental Europe. At the heart of any new policy, the mechanisms for safe and legal routes to claim asylum in the UK should be front and centre. 
2. I think the UK has been a world leader on asylum for Syrian, Afgan and Ukrainian refugees and we should be proud of that. We have made it very easy from countries such as this, and there is an argument that says that there wouldn't be the boats crossing the channel if we made it easier, but I'm not sure about that. To my mind, the calais problem is more economic migrants than asylum seekers, as they are already in a safe country.
3. No. The system needs tightening and only those who seek genuine asylum should have it granted. There should be tougher penalties for those who claim asylum unlawfully. The whole system requires a revamp in my opinion but not to make it easier as this could be easily exploited. It is important however those who genuinely need asylum are granted it. 
4. I believe that it should, but circumstances should be reviewed constantly to ensure that once a country returns to stability, or that the situation that allowed for asylum has been resolved, then that opportunity should be reviewed, and ended if deemed resolved enough. This would allow for those genuinely in need to escape a life threatening situation, however would recognise that a country would not be able to keep their borders open indefinitely.

A scheme should also be created to support families that take in asylum seekers, essentially an extension of the current system for Ukraine refugees, to assist with extra costs locally to support those helping those in need.
5. From I purely economic very point we need immigration into the UK.  If these immigrants are asylum seekers this is a benefit both to the asylum seeker and to the country.

A small group of people each wrote an opinion on the question below.

Question: Is it a good thing that people are now living to 100 or more?

Opinions:
1. in some ways its good as we only live once so to live longer is better but I worry about the quality of life as you start to get older and get ill and less mobile. Its also very expensive for the health service if people live to 100.
2. I believe it is a good thing that people are living to 100 or more as provided we are in good health and have a good quality of life, no one wants to die!  This shows the advances in modern medicine and helps keep memories of days gone by alive.  The downsides are obviously the drain on the healthcare system and the welfare state.  It is only good to live to a ripe old age if you have a good quality of life and society can afford to keep you comfortable.  If an aging population means that the state cannot support anyone who needs help, not just the aged then an aging population may not be a good thing.
3. I can only say that it is a good thing that people can now live to the age of 100 and more because it means that our healthcare and diet are getting better. There are arguments to be made that living to 100 is not always a good thing because we become a lot less able to do things at that age but the way I understand it, we would be in the same position but at 80 years old instead of 100 in the past. I think it is a good thing that our bodies are able to live so long.
4. I believe it is a good thing that people are now living to 100 or more due to the fact that people are able to spent more time alive. Due to the life expectancy being higher i assume that people face less illnesses than previously which is a positive to people. I can see how living longer can be a negative to the economy and while people are living longer, their quality of life at the later stages of their life may not be that high. However, i think that any increase in life expectancy is good overall.
5. Living to 100 or more is a good reflection on the greater health we enjoy now.  Old people are still able to make a contribution to society.  Many find it to be a fulfilling period in their lives, enjoying their grand-children and great-grandchildren, with opportunities to pass on their many years of accumulated wisdom.

Question: Should the government provide universal free childcare from birth?

Opinions:
1. The government should provide universal free childcare, but not necessarily from birth. High quality childcare allows parents to work, making use of their skills and experience and contributing to the economy. It also provides children with a positive environment in which to learn and to develop social skills. However, I do not necessarily support providing this childcare from birth. Babies benefit from having a consistent primary caregiver in their early months, and parents benefit from the opportunity to bond with their babies and to recover from the physical changes caused by birth and from the social changes caused by having a new family member. For this reason, I would support the government providing universal paid parental leave from birth, and providing universal free childcare from, say, 6 months old. I would also offer parents the opportunity to either use free childcare between 6 months and 1 year, or to have paid parental leave for the same period.

I think that some free childcare should be available to all children once they reach three, as long as it is in a setting which provides education as well as childcare.
3. Given that most parents both need to work, in most instances free childcare would be of a huge advantage to younger demographic groups. Question: Is it okay for the government to prohibit people from traveling to countries that are deemed unsafe?

Opinions:
1. I personally believe that it is okay for the government to0 prohibit people from traverlling to countries that are deemed unsafe. Realistically, if someone were to happen to its own citizens abroad in an unsafe country, they would ultimately have the blame for letting this happen. Their ultimate priority should be the safety of its citizens. However, the government would need to come up with a proper definition of 'unsafe' for this to come in effect properly.
2. I'm not too sure on this one - on one hand, yes, people should be advised when entering e.g. war zones (either global/or civil) but at the same time, I think freedom of movement is equally important. 
3. The first duty of any government should be to protect its citizens and preventing people from putting themselves in danger is one way of doing this. The government will almost certainly be more fully informed of situations in countries that make it dangerous for citizens of certain other countries to travel there. If anyone puts themselves in danger then the government will be expected to aid their citizens in other countries, preventing people from harm in the first place is essentially doing exactly that.
4. If people ignored warnings then they may end up needing the British Embassy (or similar) to assist them. It would just be easier to ban them from going. 
5. The government has a responsibility to the people in its country to warn them of places that are unsafe and give advice to restrict travel to places that are deemed unsafe. The restriction of movement should, however, be taken very seriously and only done when absolutely necessary so as not to impede human rights.
